records.title: Record northeast Pacific marine heatwave rivals the Blob and persists off the US West Coast into 2026
records.description: NOAA Fisheries reports that a marine heatwave first tracked in May 2025 reached a record average northeast Pacific temperature of 20.6 C on 9 September 2025 and has dominated West Coast waters since, strengthening again after weakening in autumn. NOAA says its ecological impact has so far been much less than the 2013 to 2016 Blob, but harmful algal blooms, reduced salmon ocean survival and unusual species locations are being tracked. The tracker records 2026 daily sea-surface temperature records at some California Current sites.

location.name: California Current and offshore northeast Pacific
location.type: Marine heatwave footprint (open coast and offshore)
location.detail: US West Coast from Southern California to Alaska and British Columbia, extending offshore across the North Pacific; Oregon and Washington nearshore waters largely spared in 2025.

records.layer_rationale: A physical ocean-temperature anomaly driven by persistent atmospheric conditions.

notes.harm: NOAA says the event has had much less ecological impact than the Blob so far, but is tracking harmful algal blooms that sicken marine mammals and reduced salmon ocean survival (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: NOAA lists shellfish fishery closures from harmful algal blooms as a possible consequence and notes lower salmon survival (ref 1); no specific closure is cited, so limited.
notes.scale: NOAA Blobtracker put the early September 2025 footprint near 3 million square miles, reaching from Kamchatka to California (ref 3), so basin-scale.
notes.duration: Tracked since May 2025; NOAA says it has dominated West Coast waters since summer 2025 and strengthened again after receding in October and November (ref 1); the tracker was updated in September 2026 with the heatwave still expanding (ref 2).
notes.significance: NOAA Fisheries published a formal feature story and maintains an operational tracker designating the event NEP25A (refs 1, 2); no emergency declaration cited.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: On 9 September 2025 the northeast Pacific reached its highest average temperature on record, 20.6 C (about 69 F), nearly half a degree warmer than any previous record (NOAA Fisheries).

records.title: Recurring Gulf of Alaska marine heatwaves weaken nutrient-carrying eddies; a new heatwave formed offshore in May 2026
records.description: A Brown University study summarised by NOAA Climate.gov found that marine heatwaves in the Gulf of Alaska have become more frequent since 2013 and weaken coastal circulation and eddies that carry nutrients to phytoplankton. NOAA's heatwave tracker reports that a second 2026 feature, NEP26A, formed in the offshore Gulf of Alaska in May 2026, and NOAA noted unusual tuna catches in Alaska in autumn 2025.

location.type: Subarctic continental shelf and offshore waters
location.detail: Alaska's Gulf of Alaska coast and offshore waters; the Bering Sea is a separate unit.

records.layer_rationale: A physical warming and circulation change with food-web consequences.

notes.harm: Climate.gov reports heatwaves reduce eddy formation and nutrient support for phytoplankton, the base of the food web; no mortality event is cited (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Climate.gov refers generally to lasting effects on fisheries (ref 1) and NOAA notes unusual tuna catches in Alaska (ref 4), but no closure or restriction is documented.
notes.scale: The study covers the Gulf of Alaska basin and the tracker places NEP26A in the offshore Gulf of Alaska region (refs 1, 2), a regional-sea extent.
notes.duration: Climate.gov states heatwaves have become more frequent since 2013 (ref 1), and large North Pacific heatwaves have occurred every year from 2019 to 2025 (ref 3).
notes.significance: Findings rest on a peer-reviewed study and agency tracker; no notice, listing or declaration is cited.

records.title: Surf and bluff erosion repeatedly close the LOSSAN rail line at San Clemente and threaten the Del Mar bluffs
records.description: The coastal rail line through San Clemente has faced repeated closures over five years from surf on one side and fragile bluffs on the other; emergency work in April 2025 halted trains for about six weeks, and high surf eroded ballast again in June and July 2026. The city faces a sand deficit of about 3 million cubic yards, and officials are studying moving the line inland. At Del Mar, about 1.7 miles of track follows a fragile bluff and stabilization is underway.

records.title: Pacifica pier closed and cafe demolished as seawall fails; local emergency declared over coastal erosion
records.description: The Pacifica Municipal Pier closed indefinitely in June 2026 after structural cracking at the seawall connection, and the city demolished the Chit Chat Cafe at its entrance. The city council declared a local emergency, and the city says erosion had already forced demolition of three apartment buildings. Rep. Sam Liccardo says $50 million for the more than $80 million seawall project was revoked in 2025, and Pacifica has received no funding for it.

records.title: Quinault Nation relocates Taholah lower village uphill from sea-level rise, storm surge and tsunami risk
records.description: The Quinault Indian Nation is moving its two villages at the Quinault River mouth about a mile uphill because of rising seas, flooding, storm surge and tsunami risk. The relocation is estimated to cost about $100 million; a $25 million federal grant and HUD housing funds for six elder homes were announced in 2022 and 2024. The tribe says relocating a whole village will take a long time.

records.title: Record king tides and storm flood Highway 101 and Marin communities in San Francisco Bay, January 2026

An $18 million federal grant for a neighborhood sheet-pile wall has been paused for months.

records.title: Aging coastal levees at Stanwood and Grays Harbor face king-tide flood risk as federal funding stalls
records.description: A January 2026 king tide gouged a half-mile of the century-old levee at Stanwood on Skagit Bay, and emergency repairs were funded in July 2026 with $1.75 million. At Grays Harbor, a planned 11-mile levee for Aberdeen and Hoquiam awaits promised federal funds after FEMA cancelled its BRIC program in April 2025 and a federal judge ordered it restored. NOAA researchers put the chance of a very strong El Nino by autumn 2026 at 80 percent, which UW oceanographer Ian Miller says can raise Pacific Northwest sea levels.

notes.significance: A federal judge ordered FEMA's cancelled BRIC program restored in December 2025, and Stanwood repairs received emergency approvals (ref 1).

records.title: Near-bottom hypoxia now covers up to 56 percent of the Oregon and Washington shelf in strong upwelling years
records.description: A 2024 Scientific Reports study found near-bottom hypoxia over about 15,500 square kilometres, nearly half the shelf inshore of 200 metres, in summer 2021, with the hypoxic share up from an average of about 2 percent in 1950 to 1980 and 24 percent in 2009 to 2018. Researchers tie the trend to stronger upwelling winds under climate change. NOAA notes hypoxic zones are increasingly forming on Dungeness crab and other fishing grounds.

location.name: Oregon and Washington continental shelf
location.detail: Near-bottom waters inshore of the 200 m isobath off Oregon and Washington, with a mid-shelf band extending 450 km along north-central Oregon and Washington.

records.layer_rationale: Declining dissolved oxygen is a physical ocean-chemistry change with ecosystem effects.

notes.harm: Barth et al. measured oxygen below the harmful 61 micromoles per kilogram threshold across 15,500 square kilometres in 2021 (refs 1, 2); the Daily Astorian reported fish and crab trapped and dying (ref 4).
notes.livelihoods: NCCOS says hypoxic zones are forming on once-productive fishing grounds and the Oregon Dungeness fishery averages $39.5 million a year (ref 3); the Quinault Nation closed crab season early in 2018 (ref 5).
notes.scale: The hypoxic band spans the shelf from Oregon into Washington, about 450 km along the coast (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Oxygen maps from 1950 show a steady decline, and hypoxia has formed nearly every summer since 2002 (refs 1, 5).
notes.significance: NOAA's Integrated Ecosystem Assessment published the finding, and NOAA funded a sensor project from 2018 to 2025 (refs 1, 3); no regulatory action.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The hypoxic fraction of near-bottom shelf water rose from about 2% (1950 to 1980) to 24% (2009 to 2018) and reached 56% in 2021 (Barth et al., Scientific Reports 2024).

records.description: Between the 1930s and 1972 Montrose Chemical's DDT acid waste and other industrial waste was dumped in deep basins between Palos Verdes and Santa Catalina Island.
